meta.blurb: Nadia owns a small bakery and still wonders what her life is for. So do a bus driver, a cleaner, a retired engineer and a teenager. Together they find that purpose grows when it reaches beyond yourself, with or without faith.
meta.bible: Nadia: a baker who owns a small bakery on a busy street; she rises at four to bake; her assistant is Dev; her brother is Farid; her mother is Leila. Walter: a retired factory worker on a small pension who lives alone, buys day-old bread from Nadia, later gives her a jar of plum jam and spends a week in hospital. Dev: Nadia's young assistant at the bakery. Joseph: a bus driver who has driven the number nine bus for eleven years and knows his passengers by name; his older brother and he stopped speaking nine years ago after a quarrel about money; he has a teenage daughter. Hana: a young woman with a pushchair whom Joseph helps one morning; she later gets her job. Mei: a hospital cleaner who once spent a frightening year in hospital as a young woman and now cleans the same wards, usually on night shift. Samuel: a retired engineer who designed bridges for forty years and a widower; his wife Ruth died last winter; he mends bicycles with teenagers on Saturdays in a church garage. Leo: a thirteen-year-old boy next door who first asks Samuel to fix his bicycle. Grace: a sixteen-year-old girl who loves books; she sits with a new girl, Yasmin, at lunch and starts a reading club for younger children at the local library. Yasmin: the new girl at Grace's school. Key terms: Purpose, Gift, Service, Community, Legacy, Ripple, Humility. Places: the community hall with its Tuesday supper; the church garage; the local library; the number nine bus route. The book speaks to You with warmth and plain words. It is respectful of every faith and of people with none: it says that many traditions teach this, never that one is right. Voice: gentle, practical, honest, never preachy. No invented studies, numbers or quotes. It is general encouragement, not a replacement for a doctor or counsellor.

beats.scene: A woman stands on a hill at sunrise looking down at a waking town
beats.summary: Nearly everyone asks at some point what their life is for, and this book helps you search for your own answer.

beats.scene: A paper map with a destination circled beside a compass
beats.summary: A goal is something you finish, while a purpose is a direction that guides many goals.

beats.scene: A bus driver greets an elderly passenger at the open doors in the rain
beats.summary: A purpose bigger than you does not need fame, because small lives can carry large meaning.

beats.scene: Hands from different cultures hold a lit candle, a book and an open bowl
beats.summary: Many faiths and philosophies teach that a good life looks beyond the self.

beats.scene: A woman sits awake at a window at night while the street sleeps
beats.summary: Questions about purpose often arrive at turning points, such as a loss, a birthday or a sleepless night.

beats.scene: A man at a desk piled with papers, clock showing very late
beats.summary: Being busy is not the same as living with purpose, because you can run fast in the wrong direction.

beats.scene: Three different doors in a row: a shop, a school and a home
beats.summary: A purpose is not a job title or a single dream, and many people live one without ever naming it.

beats.scene: Five people stand together at a bus stop at dawn
beats.summary: The book follows five ordinary people, Nadia, Joseph, Mei, Samuel and Grace, as they search for what their lives are for.

beats.scene: An open notebook and a pencil on a kitchen table at dawn
beats.summary: Each chapter gives one idea and one small exercise, and you will need only a notebook and a pencil.

beats.scene: A hand writing in a notebook, a tea cup steaming beside it
beats.summary: The first exercise is to recall the last time you felt truly useful and to write down what you were doing.

beats.scene: A baker pulls trays of golden loaves from a glowing oven before sunrise
beats.summary: Nadia rises at four every morning to bake, and her small bakery is loved by the whole street.

beats.scene: Nadia stands alone in her tidy bakery after closing time, looking tired
beats.summary: Nadia's bakery is a success, yet she feels strangely empty.

beats.scene: Nadia in a plain apron stands in a small empty shop, ten years earlier
beats.summary: Ten years ago Nadia left a job in a big factory kitchen to open her own bakery, and now she has everything she planned for.

beats.scene: Friends at a table smile at Nadia while she looks down at her plate
beats.summary: People tell Nadia she should be happy, and she feels guilty for feeling empty.

beats.scene: A shiny new oven in the bakery while Nadia looks at it without joy
beats.summary: Nadia buys a new oven and plans a holiday, but each new thing satisfies her only for a few days.

beats.scene: Nadia hands a warm loaf to an old man at the back door
beats.summary: Nadia notices an old man who buys only day-old bread and begins to quietly help him.

beats.scene: An old man in a cap stands at the shop door
beats.summary: Nadia learns that the old man is called Walter, a retired factory worker who lives alone on a small pension.

beats.scene: A fresh roll tucked into a paper bag in a baker's hand
beats.summary: Each day Nadia slips a fresh roll into Walter's bag, and he tips his cap but they never speak of it.

beats.scene: Dev in an apron laughs as Nadia hums while wrapping a loaf
beats.summary: Dev, her assistant, remarks that Nadia hums whenever she gives something away, and she realises when she is happiest.

beats.scene: Nadia sits on a crate in the back room with a notebook
beats.summary: For the first time Nadia asks herself a real question: who is this bakery for?

beats.scene: A girl notices a neighbour carrying heavy shopping up a long staircase
beats.summary: A purpose often begins when you notice what other people need.

beats.scene: A crowd of commuters stares at phones while a child watches a bird
beats.summary: Attention is rare and valuable, so it helps to look up from screens and worries and see the people around you.

beats.scene: Nadia walks down her street with her head up, notebook in hand
beats.summary: For one week Nadia watches her own street carefully and writes down what she sees.

beats.scene: A student counts coins at a bakery counter while a queue waits
beats.summary: A student counts her coins for a small loaf, and a young mother skips her own lunch, so Nadia sees a pattern.

beats.scene: A long street full of people, with one small figure circled in a notebook
beats.summary: Needs are everywhere and you cannot meet them all, so look for the one need that moves you most.

beats.scene: A notebook open with three question marks drawn in the margin
beats.summary: Three useful questions are what troubles you, what delights you, and what you could offer.

beats.scene: Nadia leans over the counter to talk quietly with Walter
beats.summary: Nadia asks Walter what he would like rather than guessing, and he says he has always loved dark rye bread.

beats.scene: A small basket by the door with a handwritten card
beats.summary: Nadia sets a basket by the door with a card inviting people to take what they need or leave what they can.

beats.scene: Two people sit close at a table, one speaking and one listening
beats.summary: Listening to people's stories reveals needs that a glance would miss.

beats.scene: A person walking in a park with a notebook, noting three things
beats.summary: The exercise is to take a ten-minute walk and write down three needs that you notice.

beats.scene: A man chops vegetables for a neighbour, while a woman plays the violin nearby
beats.summary: Your gifts are the things you do easily that others find hard, and they hint at your purpose.

beats.scene: A person lifts a heavy box effortlessly while another struggles beside them
beats.summary: Gifts hide in plain sight, and we undervalue them because they feel easy to us.

beats.scene: Dev and Nadia talk across a flour-dusted table, steam rising from tea
beats.summary: Nadia asks Dev what people come to her for, and he says she makes everyone feel at home.

beats.scene: Four small pictures: a calm face, a laugh, a list, an ear
beats.summary: Gifts are not only talents: patience, humour, calm in a crisis and a good memory for names all count.

beats.scene: Joseph the bus driver smiles at a child who waves from a window seat
beats.summary: Joseph's gift is steady kindness, and he uses it every day on his route.

beats.scene: Joseph at the wheel of a green bus at dawn, greeting early passengers
beats.summary: Joseph's day begins at six, when the number nine bus fills with nurses, students and cleaners he knows well.

beats.scene: A woman cries quietly in a window seat while the driver dims the radio
beats.summary: Joseph notices a passenger crying, and without a word he turns the radio down and lets her have the quiet.

beats.scene: A small plant growing tall toward the light beside a tight bud
beats.summary: A gift grows when it is used and shrinks when it is hidden, much like a muscle.

beats.scene: A loaf of bread broken in half and held out by two hands
beats.summary: Gifts are given to be given away, as a loaf of bread is made to be shared.

beats.scene: A list of three gifts written in a notebook with names beside them
beats.summary: The exercise is to list three gifts and name a person who could use each one this week.

beats.scene: A cleaner polishes a hospital corridor while a patient watches from a bed
beats.summary: Ordinary work can be a form of service when you do it for the people it helps.

beats.scene: Mei pushes a cleaning trolley along an empty hospital corridor at night
beats.summary: Mei works the night shift, when the hospital hums quietly and few people notice the cleaners.

beats.scene: Mei wipes a bedside table gently while a nervous family sits waiting
beats.summary: Mei, who was once a long-term patient, uses what she suffered to comfort frightened families.

beats.scene: Mei hands a warm blanket to a family sitting outside a ward
beats.summary: One night Mei brings a warm blanket to a frightened family and sits with them for a minute.

beats.scene: A single question mark glowing above a plain wooden desk
beats.summary: One question can change any job: who is this work for?

beats.scene: A driver, a clerk, a farmer and a builder stand shoulder to shoulder
beats.summary: Many jobs serve people who never see you, such as the driver, the clerk, the farmer and the builder.

beats.scene: Nadia places a warm loaf into a worker's bag at the counter
beats.summary: Nadia realises that she is not selling bread but feeding people before they face a long day.

beats.scene: A signpost with two arrows pointing in opposite directions
beats.summary: A job that harms others cannot be made good by a good attitude, so if your conscience says leave, listen.

beats.scene: A desk tidied neatly with a note for the next person
beats.summary: When you cannot change your job, you can change how you do it, with a greeting, a clean desk or a patient word.

beats.scene: A hand ticking one task from a list on a small card
beats.summary: The exercise is to choose one task today, name who it serves and do it for them.

beats.scene: A page split into a list of wants and a list of values
beats.summary: Wants change quickly, whereas values are the deeper things you care about, and purpose grows from values.

beats.scene: A new phone on one side and a group of friends on the other
beats.summary: A want might be a new phone, while the value beneath it might be staying close to the people you love.

beats.scene: A person looks back at two memories, one proud and one angry
beats.summary: To find your values, remember a time you felt proud and a time you felt angry, because both show what you care about.

beats.scene: Two columns in a notebook: wants on the left, values on the right
beats.summary: Nadia writes two lists, with bigger shops, awards and praise as wants, and generosity, craft and belonging as values.

beats.scene: Samuel stands on a bridge at dusk, one hand on the cold railing
beats.summary: Samuel's values were always to build things that last and to protect strangers who would never know his name.

beats.scene: Two roads in a field, one marked honest, the other marked kind
beats.summary: Values can conflict, as honesty and kindness sometimes do, and wisdom is choosing carefully between them.

beats.scene: A compass needle pointing north beside a long road
beats.summary: A value is a direction rather than a finish line, so you never finish being kind.

beats.scene: Joseph holds the bus doors open for a woman slowly crossing with a stick
beats.summary: Joseph arrives two minutes late because he waits for a woman with a stick, and he does not regret it.

beats.scene: Hands from many nations hold the same simple words written on cards
beats.summary: Many traditions share core values such as honesty, mercy, justice and kindness, which gives common ground to people who differ.

beats.scene: A hand circles three words from a long list of values
beats.summary: The exercise is to write ten values, then cross out seven and keep your top three.

beats.scene: Many hands pass stones along a line to build a stone wall
beats.summary: A purpose is shared, because no one builds a meaningful life entirely alone.

beats.scene: People of all ages sit in a circle in a community hall, sharing tea
beats.summary: Joining a community gives your purpose company, encouragement and a place to act.

beats.scene: A bright community hall with long tables, lanterns and steaming dishes
beats.summary: Nadia goes to the Tuesday supper at the community hall, where people of all ages share tea and food.

beats.scene: Nadia stands near the hall door holding her basket and glancing at the exit
beats.summary: Nadia feels awkward as a newcomer and nearly leaves, but she stays.

beats.scene: Joseph introduces Mei to Nadia across a table of bowls
beats.summary: Joseph is there and introduces Nadia to Mei, and they discover how their different jobs touch the same people.

beats.scene: Four hands rest together on a table: young, old, strong and tired
beats.summary: A community gives you company, encouragement, honest correction and fresh ideas.

beats.scene: A notice board crowded with posters for clubs, choirs and volunteer groups
beats.summary: To find your people, look at clubs, faith groups, volunteer teams and neighbourhood projects.

beats.scene: A group of very different people lifting one long table together
beats.summary: People of different ages and beliefs can work together, because their different gifts make the team stronger.

beats.scene: A stranger carrying a stack of chairs in a community hall
beats.summary: Do not wait to be invited, because you belong by contributing, so offer to set out the chairs.

beats.scene: A calendar with one Tuesday circled in blue ink
beats.summary: The exercise is to visit one group this month and go back a second time before you decide.

beats.scene: A hero's statue crumbles while a small hand pulls weeds nearby
beats.summary: Humility means serving without needing to be the hero, and it keeps purpose healthy.

beats.scene: A tall hero's statue with a small figure quietly weeding below it
beats.summary: Helping can slowly become about the helper, because the need to be needed is a trap.

beats.scene: Nadia frowns at the counter as Walter leaves without saying thank you
beats.summary: Nadia catches herself feeling annoyed when Walter does not thank her, and she wonders why it matters so much.

beats.scene: Walter holds out a small jar of plum jam to Nadia across the counter
beats.summary: Walter brings Nadia a jar of his late wife's plum jam, and she learns that receiving is also a way of giving.

beats.scene: Two people carry a heavy sack together, side by side
beats.summary: Serve alongside people rather than above them, and ask what would actually help.

beats.scene: A cheerful stranger receives applause while a volunteer washes dishes behind her
beats.summary: At the hall supper someone else is thanked for the work Nadia helped to do, and she is content to keep washing dishes.

beats.scene: A woman looks at a phone full of other people's celebrations while sitting alone
beats.summary: Comparing your purpose with other people's will only make you restless.

beats.scene: Grace lies in bed at night, her face lit by a phone
beats.summary: Grace scrolls her phone at night and sees friends' best moments, and she feels small by comparison.

beats.scene: A bright stage seen from the front and a messy backstage seen from behind
beats.summary: We compare our whole life with other people's best days, which is an unfair comparison.

beats.scene: A hand slips an envelope under a door while no one watches
beats.summary: The exercise is to do one kind act this week that nobody will ever know about.

beats.scene: Samuel sits in an empty garden holding tea and a photo
beats.summary: Retired and widowed, Samuel feels that his purpose has ended.

beats.scene: A second teacup set out beside a chair that no one uses
beats.summary: Samuel still makes two cups of tea each morning out of habit, and he leaves Ruth's chair as it was.

beats.scene: A dusty workbench with tools hanging in neat rows in a garage
beats.summary: When your purpose is tied to a title, it can leave with the title, and Samuel wonders who he is without his work.

beats.scene: A thirteen-year-old boy wheels a bicycle with a loose chain up a path
beats.summary: Leo, a boy from next door, knocks on Samuel's door because his bicycle chain keeps slipping.

beats.scene: Samuel and Leo kneel by a bicycle wheel, hands blackened with oil
beats.summary: Samuel mends the chain and explains each step, and it is the first time in weeks that he smiles.

beats.scene: Samuel and a group of teenagers repair bicycles in a garage
beats.summary: Samuel starts teaching young people to repair bicycles and finds that his skills still matter.

beats.scene: Ten teenagers around rows of bicycles in a bright church garage
beats.summary: Every Saturday the church garage fills with teenagers, bicycles and the smell of oil, and Samuel shows them how to straighten a bent wheel.

beats.scene: Samuel laughs with a group of teenagers over a plate of biscuits
beats.summary: Teaching changes Samuel, because he learns patience and discovers that the young people teach him too.

beats.scene: A retired engineer stands proudly beside a line of repaired bicycles
beats.summary: A purpose does not retire but changes shape, so Samuel's skills of measuring and caring are still in use.

beats.scene: A person looks at a list of roles crossed out one by one
beats.summary: The exercise is to imagine your role ended tomorrow and to ask which part of it you could still give.

beats.scene: A notebook open on a table with a clock and a daily schedule
beats.summary: How you spend your days shows what you truly serve, so look honestly at your calendar.

beats.scene: A week of seven columns on a page, each filled with coloured blocks
beats.summary: To audit your week, write down each day in blocks of work, sleep, screens and time with other people.

beats.scene: Nadia studies a notebook page where every block is labelled bakery
beats.summary: Nadia sees that almost every hour of her week belongs to the bakery, with none left for the people she wants to help.

beats.scene: A clock whose face is divided into small bright wedges
beats.summary: Twenty minutes a day adds up to more than two hours a week, so small blocks of time are enough.

beats.scene: A kettle boiling beside a person who types a short message
beats.summary: Attach a purpose to an existing habit, such as writing a kind message while the kettle boils.

beats.scene: A page with a single clear sentence written in the centre
beats.summary: Reducing your purpose to one sentence gives clarity and a way to decide between competing demands.

beats.scene: A person writes one line on a card by a window at dawn
beats.summary: Try writing your purpose as one clear sentence, and expect to revise it.

beats.scene: Nadia crosses out a long grand sentence and writes a shorter one
beats.summary: Nadia's first draft is too grand, so she rewrites it as a modest promise to give her street a warm start to the day.

beats.scene: A woman tests a handwritten card against a checklist on a kitchen table
beats.summary: Test your sentence: it should include other people, it should be something you can do today, and it should fit your values.

beats.scene: A sentence taped to a fridge door beside a child's drawing
beats.summary: The exercise is to write your sentence, test it, tape it to the fridge, and remember that Mei's is to help frightened people feel less alone.

beats.scene: A person sits on a bed in early light, eyes closed
beats.summary: A short morning pause helps you start the day aware of your purpose.

beats.scene: A person sits with eyes closed, breathing slowly beside an open window
beats.summary: In the morning pause, take three slow breaths and ask yourself who you might serve today.

beats.scene: Hands folded in prayer beside hands resting on knees in silent thought
beats.summary: Prayer, meditation or silent reflection can deepen purpose, in whatever form suits you.

beats.scene: A still room with a window, a plain chair and a small lit candle
beats.summary: Silence is not empty but full of what the noise of the day hides from us.

beats.scene: Joseph sits in his bus in an empty depot, hands resting on the wheel
beats.summary: Before his first run, Joseph sits in the cab for one minute and thinks about the people he will carry.

beats.scene: Nadia lays her hands on a tray of warm loaves before the shop opens
beats.summary: Before opening, Nadia stands by the warm loaves and names three customers she hopes to cheer.

beats.scene: A person writes in a small notebook by lamplight at night
beats.summary: An evening review of where you helped and where you did not builds wisdom over time.

beats.scene: A page torn gently from a notebook and folded away
beats.summary: Forgive yourself for the chances you missed, learn from them, and let them go.

beats.scene: A notebook with a short handwritten entry and a pen beside it
beats.summary: A short notebook habit of a few lines each day helps you see your own progress over weeks.

beats.scene: A week of small marks beside morning and evening boxes
beats.summary: The exercise is to try seven days of two minutes each morning and each evening, and then notice what changes.

beats.scene: Joseph helps a young woman lift a pushchair onto his crowded bus
beats.summary: Small acts matter, because they change a real person's day.

beats.scene: Joseph lifts a pushchair onto his crowded bus for a hurrying woman
beats.summary: Joseph helps Hana lift her pushchair onto his crowded bus, and she is rushing to a job interview.

beats.scene: Ripples spreading outward on a pond from a single falling drop
beats.summary: Kindness spreads in ripples that you may never see.

beats.scene: A seed falling from a branch into a field of waving grass
beats.summary: You may never see the results of your kindness, just as a gardener plants seeds whose flowers he may not see.

beats.scene: Hana smiles at Joseph on the bus a year later, holding a child's hand
beats.summary: A year later Hana boards Joseph's bus again and tells him that his kindness that morning kept her from giving up.

beats.scene: A child watches a parent hold the door open for a stranger
beats.summary: Children learn what matters by watching what adults do, and Nadia's customers' children watch her give.

beats.scene: A tired person climbs a long staircase carrying a heavy bag
beats.summary: Small acts are not easy, because the challenge is to do them again on tired days.

beats.scene: A coin and a small clock placed side by side on a table
beats.summary: Kindness costs a little time or comfort, and that cost is what makes it real.

beats.scene: A person turns away from a scoreboard toward an open door
beats.summary: Do not measure the results too closely, but simply do the next kind thing in front of you.

beats.scene: Three small stones laid in a row on a windowsill
beats.summary: The exercise is to perform three small acts this week and then let them go without waiting for any result.

beats.scene: A woman stares at a wall calendar with a blank evening, looking uncertain
beats.summary: Doubt is normal, since a purpose is not a feeling you will have every day.

beats.scene: A person stands at a window in grey rain, hands wrapped around a mug
beats.summary: Feelings are like the weather, which changes, while purpose is more like a direction that you keep.

beats.scene: Nadia kneads sticky dough in a grey dawn, her face tired
beats.summary: One grey morning Nadia doubts everything, but she bakes anyway and her mood lifts by lunchtime.

beats.scene: A bus travelling the same route past the same shops in the rain
beats.summary: Joseph has driven the same route thousands of times, and he finds that repetition is where character forms.

beats.scene: Mei folds a white uniform in a locker, a long list on the wall
beats.summary: Mei starts taking extra shifts and visiting patients on her days off, until her schedule has no space left.

beats.scene: Mei sits on a hospital bench with her head in her hands, exhausted
beats.summary: Mei burns out from giving too much, and she learns that rest is part of her purpose.

beats.scene: Mei walks beside a slow river in the morning light
beats.summary: Mei takes a week off to sleep and walk by the river, and she discovers that the hospital goes on without her.

beats.scene: A relay baton passing from one hand to another on a track
beats.summary: You are not the only helper in the world, and other people can carry the work too.

beats.scene: Mei sits with Joseph at the hall, her head resting on her hand
beats.summary: Mei admits to Joseph how tired she has been, and he gladly helps; asking for help is a gift to others.

beats.scene: A list headed what fills me up, with a lamp drawn beside it
beats.summary: The exercise is to list what refills you, and to see a doctor or counsellor if a low mood lasts for weeks.

beats.scene: A woman holds up a hand to politely refuse a long list of requests
beats.summary: Saying no to some things protects your ability to say yes to your real purpose.

beats.scene: Nadia reads a long list of event requests at her counter
beats.summary: Nadia is asked to cater five events and run a festival stall, and she is flattered but remembers her sentence.

beats.scene: Nadia hands a kind refusal note across a counter with a smile
beats.summary: To say no kindly, thank the person, be honest and brief, and do not pile up long excuses.

beats.scene: A person sits quietly after a phone call, a hand on their chest
beats.summary: Guilt after a refusal is normal, and it fades much faster than the resentment of an unwanted yes.

beats.scene: A phone left face down in a basket beside a bright window
beats.summary: You also have to say no to yourself, to scrolling and distraction that steal your attention.

beats.scene: Nadia signs a lease for a second shop, her pen hesitating over the paper
beats.summary: Out of pride, Nadia says yes to the wrong thing and opens a second bakery, telling herself it will feed more people.

beats.scene: Dev rubs his eyes by a counter in an unfamiliar shop with few customers
beats.summary: In the second shop the customers are few, the rent is high and Dev is tired, and the quality slips.

beats.scene: A closed shop window with a hand taping a sign to the door
beats.summary: Nadia's second shop fails, and she learns that failure can refine a purpose.

beats.scene: Nadia stands outside the closed shop with a bag, rain on the pavement
beats.summary: Nadia feels ashamed and imagines what the neighbours say, but Walter says that the old shop is the one he comes to.

beats.scene: A notebook page headed what I learned, with a pencil beside it
beats.summary: Failure is a rough editor, and the exercise is to recall a failure and write down what it taught you.

beats.scene: Two people argue politely across a table while a third looks on
beats.summary: Not everyone will understand your purpose, and you can listen to criticism without being controlled by it.

beats.scene: Farid sits at a family table and frowns at Nadia across the bread
beats.summary: Nadia's brother Farid tells her that she is wasting her talent by giving bread away.

beats.scene: Nadia turns a thoughtful page of her notebook at the kitchen table
beats.summary: Listen for the true part in a criticism, because your critic may be right about something.

beats.scene: Three small gates in a row, labelled true, kind and useful
beats.summary: Test criticism with three questions: is it true, is it kind, and is it useful?

beats.scene: Joseph sits at a family table while relatives point at an office job advert
beats.summary: Joseph's family wants him to take a better-paid office job, and he thanks them but chooses to stay.

beats.scene: A coin and a heart balanced on two sides of a scale
beats.summary: You can pursue a purpose and still earn a living, because the two can coexist.

beats.scene: A small shop with a till and a basket of bread for the street
beats.summary: A bakery that stays open can keep serving, so Nadia keeps her prices fair and pays Dev well.

beats.scene: A fair set of scales balancing a coin and a handshake
beats.summary: Purpose is no excuse for underpaying others or for being underpaid yourself, because justice is part of service.

beats.scene: A family around a table sharing a modest meal under a warm lamp
beats.summary: Providing for the family you love is itself a purpose, and it is nothing to be ashamed of.

beats.scene: Two friends at a table, one writing notes while the other speaks
beats.summary: The exercise is to ask one trusted person for honest feedback on how you serve, and to listen without defending.

beats.scene: A family around a kitchen table, a child helping a parent to cook
beats.summary: The home is the first place to practise purpose, with the people closest to you.

beats.scene: Nadia holds a phone to her ear while looking out over the street
beats.summary: Nadia calls her mother Leila every Sunday, and she realises how long she had given her only leftover attention.

beats.scene: Joseph and his teenage daughter at a table, a phone in a drawer
beats.summary: At home Joseph puts his phone in a drawer at dinner and gives his teenage daughter his full attention.

beats.scene: A tired person pouring the last of the soup into a bowl for guests
beats.summary: The people closest to us often receive what is left of us, so give them the first and best of your attention.

beats.scene: A heavy grey stone sits in an open coat pocket
beats.summary: A grudge is like a stone in your pocket, because the longer you carry it, the heavier it becomes.

beats.scene: Joseph and his older brother shaking hands on a doorstep after a long argument
beats.summary: Forgiving an old quarrel makes room for purpose, and Joseph makes peace with his brother.

beats.scene: Two brothers shake hands warmly, one standing on the doorstep
beats.summary: Forgiveness is not forgetting or excusing what happened, but putting down the weight, and it may take time.

beats.scene: A small gate in a fence, half open, with a lamp shining beyond
beats.summary: Forgiving someone does not mean staying close to a person who may harm you, and safety still matters.

beats.scene: Nadia says sorry to Dev across the counter, flour on both their sleeves

B1B2: Sooner or later, almost everyone asks what their life is for. This book will not hand you a ready-made answer, but it will help you search for your own.
A goal is something you can finish, like passing an exam or buying a house. A purpose is more like a compass, because it points the way for many goals.
When people hear the words big purpose, they often imagine fame, wealth or a world-changing invention. In truth, a purpose can be big in meaning while it stays quite small in size.
Many faiths and philosophies, from every part of the world, teach that a good life looks beyond the self. They use different words and stories, but they often agree on this one idea.
The question of purpose rarely arrives while life is busy and loud. It more often comes at a birthday, after a loss or during a sleepless night.
A full diary can make you feel important without making you feel useful. You can run very fast and still be heading in the wrong direction.
Your purpose is not the same as your job title or your biggest dream. Many people already live it every day without ever having a name for it.
In this book you will meet five ordinary people, and each one is still searching. Nadia bakes bread, Joseph drives a bus, Mei cleans a hospital, Samuel is retired and Grace is still at school.
Each chapter offers one idea and one small thing to try at the end. All you need is a notebook, a pencil and a little honesty.
For your first exercise, think back to the last time you felt truly useful. Write down what you were doing, who was there and why it felt good.
Nadia wakes at four every morning, long before the street is awake. By the time the sun comes up, the whole shop smells of warm bread.
Nadia owns a bakery that is loved by the whole street, and her accounts look healthy. Even so, she locks the door each evening with a strange, hollow feeling.
Ten years ago Nadia left a job in a big factory kitchen and opened her own small bakery. By most ordinary measures she has now achieved nearly everything that she once planned to do.
Her friends tell her she should be very happy, and she knows they are right. That only makes her feel guilty about the empty feeling that will not go away.
Nadia buys a new oven and books a short holiday, hoping that these will help. They give her pleasure for a few days, and then the empty feeling returns.
One morning, Nadia notices an old man who always buys the cheapest day-old bread. The next day she slips a fresh roll into his bag and says nothing.
Nadia learns that the old man is called Walter, and that he lives alone on a small pension. He worked in a factory for most of his life and now has very little money.
Every morning, Nadia slips a fresh roll into Walter's bag without saying a word. He always notices, and he tips his cap to her, but neither of them mentions it.
One day her assistant Dev says that Nadia always hums when she gives something away. She stops and realises that he is right, and that those are her happiest moments.
That night Nadia sits in the quiet shop and asks herself a new question. Who is this bakery really for, and what does it need to be?
Purpose rarely begins with a grand and carefully drawn plan. It more often begins when you look up from your own worries and notice what somebody else needs.
Most of us walk through the day with our eyes on a screen. Looking up and seeing the people around you is the first act of attention.
For one week Nadia walks her street with her head up and a small notebook in her pocket. She writes down everything she sees that someone seems to need.
One afternoon a student counts her coins and buys only the smallest loaf. Later a young mother gives her own lunch to her child, and Nadia sees a pattern.
There are far too many needs in the world for any one person to meet. Look for the one that touches your heart most and begin there.
Here are three useful questions that you can ask yourself over the next few days. What troubles me, what delights me, and what could I offer to the people who are affected?
Instead of guessing what Walter needs, Nadia simply asks him what he likes. He smiles and says he has always loved dark rye bread.
Nadia places a basket of rolls by the door with a handwritten card. It says that anyone may take what they need and leave what they can.
A glance can tell you very little about what someone needs. When you listen to their story, the real need often becomes clear.
Your exercise is to take a ten-minute walk this week with your head up. Write down three needs that you notice, and circle the one that tugs at you.
Your gifts are the things that come easily to you, though others may find them hard. They are clues, because the skills you carry usually point toward the help you can give.
Your gifts can hide in plain sight, precisely because they feel so easy to you. You may assume that everyone can do them, when in fact they cannot.
Nadia asks Dev what people come to her for. He thinks for a moment and says that she makes everyone feel at home.
Gifts are not only talents like music or sport. Patience, humour, a calm head in a crisis and a good memory for names are gifts too.
Joseph drives the number nine bus, and he knows most of his passengers by name. His gift is a steady, friendly calm, which makes strangers feel welcome before the first stop.
Joseph begins his first trip at six each morning, when the bus is full of nurses, students and cleaners. He knows where each of them gets off and how they take their tea.
One grey morning Joseph notices a passenger crying quietly in the window seat. He says nothing, but he turns down the radio and drives a little more gently.
A gift is like a muscle, because it grows stronger when you use it. If you hide it away, it slowly weakens and you may forget it was ever there.
A loaf of bread is made to be shared, and a gift is much the same. It is only truly yours once you have given some of it away.
Your exercise is to write down three of your gifts. Next to each one, name a person who could use it this week.
Ordinary work can be a kind of service, whatever your job is. A clean floor, a hot meal or a ticket handed over politely can make another person's day easier.
Mei works the night shift at the hospital, pushing her trolley through silent corridors. Hardly anyone notices a cleaner, but she is there at the hour when the fear is greatest.

Mei spent a frightening year in hospital as a young woman, and later she took a job cleaning the same wards. She remembers exactly how scared the families feel, so she always stops to speak to them kindly.
One night Mei notices a family waiting outside the ward, shivering in their thin coats. She fetches a warm blanket and sits with them for a minute.
There is one question that can change any job, which is who this work is for. Once you can name the people, the work stops being only a task.
Many jobs serve people who will never see your face, such as farming, building or driving. Each of them is a thread in the great web that keeps a town alive.
Over the next few days, Nadia begins to see her own work in a different light. She is not simply selling bread, she thinks, but sending people into a hard day with something warm inside them.
A good attitude cannot make a harmful job good. If your conscience keeps telling you that your work hurts other people, take it seriously.
If you cannot change your job at the moment, you can still change how you do it. A warm greeting, a tidy desk for the next person or a patient word can all carry meaning.
For today's exercise, pick one ordinary task from your day. Name the person it serves, and then do it as if you were doing it for them.
Wants change quickly, and what you desire today may bore you next month. Your values, such as honesty or care for others, change much more slowly, so a purpose grows best from them.
You may want the newest phone in the shop, but you may value staying close to your friends. Wants point at objects, while values point at what matters beneath them.
To find your values, remember a time you felt truly proud and a time you felt angry. Both feelings show you what you care about most.
One evening Nadia sits down and writes two separate lists in her notebook. Under wants she puts a bigger shop, praise and prizes, and under values she writes generosity, craft and belonging.
Samuel realises that he always valued building things that last. He also cared about keeping strangers safe, even though they would never know his name.
Sometimes two good values seem to pull against each other, such as honesty and kindness. Wisdom means choosing carefully, and usually you can be both truthful and gentle.
A value is a direction, not a finish line. Nobody is ever finished with being kind or honest, and that is why these values can guide a whole life.
Living by your values will sometimes cost you something, and it is honest to admit it. Joseph waits for a slow woman with a stick, arrives two minutes late and does not regret it for a second.
Many traditions around the world teach honesty, mercy, justice and kindness. Their shared values give very different people a common place to stand.
For your exercise, write down ten values that matter to you. Cross out seven of them, so that only your three most important ones remain.
Nobody builds a meaningful life completely on their own. Every one of us depends on farmers, teachers, drivers and neighbours whom we may never thank.
Find a community of people who care about something good, such as a food bank, a choir or a place of worship. They will give you company, encouragement and a real place to act.
Walter mentions a Tuesday supper at the community hall, so Nadia decides to go. She carries a basket of bread and finds long tables full of people of every age.
At first Nadia feels awkward, and she nearly turns around and goes home. Instead she takes a breath, puts the basket on the table and stays.
Joseph is at the supper too, and he introduces Nadia to Mei. They discover that their different jobs reach the same people in surprising ways.
A good community gives you company when you are tired and ideas when you are stuck. It also gives you honest correction when you are going the wrong way.
To find your people, look at the notice boards near you. Clubs, choirs, faith groups, volunteer teams and neighbourhood projects are all good places to start.
People of different ages and beliefs can work side by side. Their differences are not a problem, because different gifts make a stronger team.
Do not wait for someone to invite you to help. Offer to set out the chairs or wash the cups, and belonging will follow.
This month, visit one group that cares about something good. Go at least twice before you decide whether it is the right place for you.

Humility does not mean thinking badly of yourself or being weak. It means that you can serve without needing applause, and that you are happy when the work succeeds even if someone else gets the credit.
Helping can slowly become about the helper instead of the person in need. The wish to be thanked, admired or needed can quietly take over.
One morning Walter forgets to say thank you, and Nadia is annoyed for hours. She wonders why it bothers her so much, since she meant to give in secret.
The next day Walter brings her a jar of plum jam made from his late wife's recipe. Nadia understands that letting him give something back is a kindness too.
Try to serve alongside people as an equal, rather than from above them. Ask what would really help, and then listen to the answer before you act.
At the next supper, a visitor thanks someone else for the soup that Nadia mostly made. She smiles, picks up a tea towel and goes on drying the dishes.
It is easy to compare your quiet life with someone else's exciting one. But a purpose is not a race, and nobody else can live the life that was given to you.
Late at night Grace looks at her phone and sees her friends' holidays, parties and prizes. She puts it down feeling smaller than she did an hour before.
When you compare yourself with others, you compare your whole life with their best days. That is never a fair match, and you will always lose.
This week, do one kind thing that nobody will ever know about. Notice how it feels to give without any applause at all.
Samuel worked as an engineer for forty years, and last winter his wife Ruth died. His days are quiet now, and he feels as if his purpose retired along with him.
Out of habit, Samuel still makes two cups of tea every morning. He pours one down the sink, and he leaves Ruth's chair exactly as it was.
Samuel's identity was wrapped up in his work, and when the job ended, he felt lost. He wonders who he is now that nobody needs his calculations.
One Saturday a boy called Leo knocks on Samuel's door, holding a bicycle with a loose chain. His mother has told him that the old engineer might be able to help.
Samuel fixes the chain on the garage floor and explains every step to Leo as he goes. By the time they finish, he has smiled for the first time in weeks.
A neighbour asks Samuel to help some teenagers repair old bicycles. He agrees, reluctantly at first, and within a month he is looking forward to every Saturday.
Every Saturday morning, about ten teenagers crowd into the garage with their bicycles. Samuel shows them how to straighten a bent wheel with nothing but a spoke key and patience.
Teaching makes Samuel more patient than he has ever been, and he learns from his pupils as well. They show him new music, new jokes and a different way of looking at old problems.
Samuel realises that a purpose does not retire when a career ends. It simply changes shape, and his careful, measuring mind is still at work.
Imagine that your main role ended tomorrow, whether it is your job, your family role or your place in a team. Write down which part of it you could still give away.
Your calendar tells the truth about what you serve. Look honestly at last week, and ask which hours helped other people and which hours were simply spent.
To audit your week, write down what you did each day in simple blocks. Show your work, sleep, errands, screens and the time you spent with other people.
Nadia looks at her week and sees that almost every hour belongs to the bakery. There is no space left for the neighbours she says she wants to help.
You do not need whole days or empty months to live your purpose. Twenty minutes a day adds up to more than two hours a week, which is enough to make a real difference.
A good way to start is to attach a small act to something you already do. You might write a kind message while the kettle boils or while you wait for the bus.
A single sentence forces you to be clear about what you are doing. It also gives you a simple way to decide between different demands on your time.
Try writing your purpose in a single sentence, for example, I want to use my skills to make people feel welcome. It will not be perfect, and you can change it as often as you like.
Nadia's first draft says she will feed the whole city, which is far too grand. She rewrites it as a promise to give her own street a warm start to the day.
Test your sentence with three simple and honest questions. Does it include other people, could you begin it today, and does it fit the values you care about most?
Write your sentence, test it with the three questions and tape it where you will see it daily. Mei's sentence, for example, is that she wants to help frightened people feel less alone.
Start each morning with a short pause of two or three minutes. Sit quietly, breathe slowly, and remind yourself what you want to give today.
During your morning pause, take three slow and steady breaths and let your shoulders drop. Then ask yourself one simple question, which is who you might be able to serve today.
People of faith may pray, and others may meditate or simply sit in silence. Whatever form you choose, the aim is the same, which is to listen more deeply than usual.
Silence is not empty, although it may feel that way at first. It lets you hear the things that daily noise covers up.
Before his first run, Joseph sits in the empty bus for one minute with his hands on the wheel. He thinks about the people he is about to carry safely through the city.
Before she unlocks the door, Nadia stands beside the warm loaves and names three customers she hopes to cheer. It takes less than a minute and changes how she serves all day.
In the evening, take two minutes to ask yourself where you helped today and where you missed a chance. The point is to learn, not to punish yourself.
When you notice a missed chance, forgive yourself and learn from it. Then let it go, because tomorrow will bring a new one.
Keep a notebook and write just a few lines each day. After several weeks you can look back and see how far you have come.
For one week, try two quiet minutes in the morning and two in the evening. At the end of the week, notice what has changed in you.
One small act of kindness will not change the world. But it can change one person's day, and that person is part of the world too.
One morning Joseph helps a young woman called Hana lift her pushchair onto his crowded bus. She is rushing to a job interview and is close to tears.
A kind word spreads like ripples on a pond. The person you help may help another, and you may never see where the ripples end.
You may never see the results of what you do. A gardener plants seeds knowing that someone else may sit in the shade one day.
A year later Hana boards Joseph's bus again and tells him what that morning meant. She had been ready to go home, but his kindness gave her the courage to get the job.
Children learn what matters by watching what adults do, not by listening to speeches. The small acts that you think nobody sees are being studied closely.
A small act of kindness is easy once and harder to repeat on a tired day. The real strength lies in doing it again and again.
Real kindness usually costs something, such as a little time, comfort or convenience. That cost is part of what makes it real.
Try not to measure the results of your kindness too closely. Simply do the next kind thing that is in front of you, and trust that it counts.
This week, do three small acts of kindness for three different people, and then let each one go. Do not wait for a reply or a sign that anybody noticed.
Some days you will wake up feeling that nothing you do matters. This is normal, because purpose is not a feeling that stays with you every single day.
Feelings change like the weather, and nobody can control them. Your purpose is more like a direction, and you can keep to it even when the sky is grey.
One grey morning Nadia wakes at four and wonders whether any of it matters. She bakes anyway, and by lunchtime the heaviness has lifted.
Joseph has driven the number nine route so many times that he could do it with his eyes closed. He has learned that repetition is where character is quietly formed.
Mei begins taking extra shifts, and she visits lonely patients on her days off. Soon her schedule has no space left in it at all.
Mei has given so much to other people that she has nothing left, and one night she falls asleep on a hospital bench. She learns that rest is not selfish, because a tired helper cannot help for long.
Mei takes a week off to sleep, to eat properly and to walk by the river. She discovers, with some surprise, that the hospital continues perfectly well without her.
You are not the only person in the world who can help. Others can carry the work too, and sometimes they will do it better.
Mei finally admits to Joseph how tired she has been, and he is glad to help. She learns that asking for help gives other people a chance to give.
Make a list of things that refill your energy, such as sleep, a walk or a meal with friends. If a low mood lasts for weeks, please see a doctor or counsellor.
Learn to say no kindly to things that are not yours to do. Every refusal protects your time and energy for the work you truly care about.
People ask Nadia to cater five events and to run a festival stall. She is flattered, but she looks at her sentence and wonders whether all of it fits.
To say no kindly, begin with thanks, then be honest and brief. Long excuses usually make the refusal harder for both people.
It is normal to feel guilty after you have said no. The guilt fades quickly, much faster than the resentment that follows an unwanted yes.
Sometimes the hardest no is the one you say to yourself. Endless scrolling and small distractions can steal the time that your purpose needs.
Because she feels proud of her success, Nadia decides to open a second bakery across the city. She tells herself that it will feed more people.
In the new shop the customers are few, the rent is high and the days are long. Dev is exhausted, and the quality of the bread begins to slip.
Nadia opens a second bakery across the city, but it closes after eight months. It hurts, yet she realises that she wanted to feed the street, not simply to grow bigger.
Nadia feels ashamed and imagines what the neighbours are saying behind her back. Then Walter appears at the old shop and tells her that it is the one he comes to.
Failure is a rough editor that cuts away what was never essential. Your exercise is to recall a failure and write down what it taught you.
Some friends and relatives will not understand your choices, and some may laugh at them. Listen when criticism is fair, but do not let every opinion steer your life.
At a family dinner, Nadia's brother Farid tells her that she is wasting her talent by giving bread away. He says it with love, but it still stings.
When someone criticises you, listen for the part that is true. Your critic may be right about something, even if the rest is unfair.
You can sort any piece of criticism by asking yourself three simple questions. Is it true, is it kind, and is it useful to me now?
Joseph's family urges him to apply for a better-paid office job. He thanks them warmly, but after some thought he decides to stay on the bus.
You may worry that a purpose means giving up your pay. In fact, most people live out their purpose while holding an ordinary job, and the two can support each other.
Nadia learns that a business which closes cannot feed anyone. She keeps her prices fair, pays Dev properly and keeps the basket by the door.
A good purpose is never an excuse for underpaying other people. Nor should you accept being treated unfairly yourself, because justice is part of service.
Providing for the family you love is itself a purpose. There is nothing small or selfish about earning money to look after your own people.
For your exercise, ask one trusted person how well they think you serve others. Listen without defending yourself, and then say thank you.
The home is often the first place to practise your purpose. Patience with a child, a phone call to an aging parent or a shared meal can all carry deep meaning.
Every Sunday evening Nadia calls her mother Leila, usually while she is tidying up the kitchen. She realises that for years she had given her only the leftovers of her attention.
At dinner Joseph puts his phone in a drawer and turns to his teenage daughter. She is surprised at first, and then she begins to talk.
The people closest to us often get what is left over after everyone else has had the best of us. Try giving them the first part of your attention instead.
An old grudge is like a stone in your pocket. The longer you carry it, the heavier it feels, and the more it slows you down.
Joseph and his brother stopped speaking after an argument about money nine years ago. He finally visits him, and the long silence breaks with a simple handshake.
Forgiveness does not mean forgetting what happened, and it does not mean saying it was acceptable. It means putting down the weight, and that can take a long time.
Forgiving someone does not mean that you must stay close to a person who might hurt you again. Your safety still matters, and wise boundaries are not unkind.
Nadia apologises to Dev for being sharp with him during the months of the second shop. He smiles and says he knew she was under pressure.
Choose one person at home and give them fifteen minutes of your full attention. If an old quarrel troubles you, write a letter that you may never send.
Write down three things each day that you are thankful for. Gratitude reminds you that you are not only giving, but also receiving, so your purpose stays light rather than heavy.
Each evening Nadia writes three things she is thankful for. Tonight they are Walter's plum jam, Dev's laugh and the warmth of the ovens on a cold morning.
Gratitude changes giving from a sacrifice into a kind of sharing. When you remember all that you have been given, you give out of fullness and not out of duty.
You can give three things, namely your time, your money and your attention. You do not need a lot of any of them, because a little given regularly goes a long way.
Samuel gives his time by offering one Saturday morning every week. It is not much, but it is regular, and the young people know they can count on him.
If you give money, choose a small regular amount that you can keep up. Check that the cause is honest and well run before you give.
Attention is perhaps the rarest gift of all, and anyone can give it. Turn the phone face down, look at the person and be fully present.
Listening is a form of service that costs nothing. When you give someone your full attention, without hurrying to fix their problem, you show them that they matter.
One night Mei sits beside a frightened old man on the ward and says very little. She only listens, and afterwards he falls peacefully asleep.
This week, give one hour of listening to someone who needs it. Do not try to fix anything or give advice unless you are asked.
Do not expect your purpose to bloom overnight, however hard you try. Like a tree, it grows slowly, and the roots are developing even when you cannot see anything above the soil.
Change on Nadia's street is slow, and she often wonders whether it is working. After a year, however, she sees more neighbours at the supper and a fuller basket by the door.
Grace is sixteen and rather shy, and she spends most afternoons reading in the local library. She wonders what a girl of her age could possibly be for.
Courage does not mean having no fear at all. It begins with one small step that you take while you are still afraid.
Grace is sixteen, and she notices that a new girl sits alone at lunch every day. Her heart is beating fast, but she walks over and sits beside her.
The new girl is called Yasmin, and she turns out to love the same books as Grace. By the end of lunch, they have already made plans to meet again.
One afternoon Yasmin points out that the younger children in the library cannot find books they enjoy. She says that Grace, who loves stories, should read to them.

Grace loves books more than anything, so she starts a small reading club for younger children at the local library. Each week she sees their faces light up, and she feels that she has found something important.
Only three children come to the first meeting, and one of them does not say a word. Grace reads with a different voice for each character, and soon all three are leaning forward.
For your exercise, do one small brave thing this week that you have been putting off. It might be a phone call, a question or an offer of help.
The way you live your purpose will change as you move through life. A young parent, a worker and a retired person may serve in different ways, though the heart of it remains the same.
As the years pass, Nadia's hands begin to ache and she can no longer lift the heavy sacks. Dev gradually takes over the ovens, and she feels a pang of loss.
Whatever you have learned in life, there is someone younger who needs it. Teaching is one of the oldest ways to give a gift that lasts.
Nadia begins teaching young people to bake on Sunday afternoons. Grace brings her reading-club children along for warm bread and stories.
Samuel still misses his wife every single day, and he does not think that will ever change. Yet he finds that his sorrow and his new purpose can sit side by side without cancelling each other.
On Ruth's birthday Samuel walks Leo across one of the bridges that he designed. He explains how it was built and why it is safe, and he feels close to her.
Walter falls ill and spends a week in the hospital where Mei works. She knows him through Nadia, and each night she brings him one of the fresh rolls.
Nadia visits Walter and finds him pale but cheerful. He tells her that the rolls were never really about the bread, but about being seen.
Hope is not just a feeling, because it is also something you can practise. On hard days, hope means doing one small, good thing and trusting that it counts.
For your exercise, write a few lines about a hard season that you have survived. Then write one small act of hope that you could do this week.
Imagine that you are one plank in a very long bridge. Many people laid planks before you, and others will lay planks after you, and the bridge still carries people across.
One Tuesday, Nadia, Joseph, Mei, Samuel and Grace find themselves at the same table at the hall supper. They realise that their lives are connected in ways they never planned.
Most of us will not be remembered by statues or history books. What lasts is the way we made people feel and the good that continues without us.
When you imagine your last days, you do not wish for a bigger bank balance or a better title. You hope that people will say you were kind and that you made their lives easier.
Some people find their purpose through religious faith, and they may feel that they are called. Others find it through reason, conscience and love, and both can walk the same road together.
The five friends do not share the same beliefs, because one prays, one doubts and one is not sure. Yet they share a table, a neighbourhood and a purpose, and none of them minds the differences.
Here is a simple plan that you can try for one week. Pause each morning, notice one need, do one small kind act, and write down three things you are thankful for each evening.
When the week is over, look back and notice what has shifted. Keep what helped, change what did not and begin another week.
Do not wait until you feel completely ready, because that day may never come. Choose one small thing that you can do before the sun goes down, and then do it.
Your purpose is bigger than you, and that is not a burden but a gift. You are part of something larger, and the world is a little better when you play your part.
C1C2: Sooner or later, usually in a quiet hour when the noise of the day has finally died away, almost everyone asks what their life is truly for. This book will not hand you a ready-made answer, because an answer borrowed from someone else rarely fits. What it can offer is a lantern, a few honest questions and the company of some ordinary people who went looking.

A goal is a place you can arrive at, tick off a list and leave behind, such as a diploma, a promotion or a house of your own. A purpose is closer to a compass, since it does not end when you arrive but keeps pointing the way. Once you know your direction, a great many separate goals begin to fall into a sensible order and a clear purpose.

Mention a great purpose and many people picture fame, a stage and a crowd, or an invention that changes the world. Yet a purpose can be vast in meaning while remaining modest in size, lived out in a kitchen, a classroom or the front seat of a bus. What makes it large is not how many people see it, but how deeply it reaches beyond your own comfort.

Across the centuries, many religions and philosophies, in every part of the world, have taught that a good life looks beyond the self. They use different languages, stories and images, and they certainly disagree about a great deal, yet they often meet on this single idea. You do not have to follow any of them to find the idea worth testing in your own days.

The question of purpose seldom knocks while life is busy, loud and going well. It tends to arrive at a milestone birthday, after a loss, or in the thin grey hour of a sleepless night when the usual distractions have fallen silent. Do not be afraid of it, because the question itself is a sign that you are paying attention to your own life.

A full diary can make you feel important without ever making you feel useful, and the two feelings are easily confused. It is quite possible to run very fast, answer every message and still be travelling in a direction that you never actually chose. Purpose asks a quieter question than busyness does, namely what all this effort is finally for.

Your purpose is not the same thing as your job title, and it is not a single glittering dream waiting at the end of a long road. Many people are already living it in small ways every day, without ever having found a name for what they are doing. Naming it simply helps you to do it on purpose, and to do more of it.

Along the way you will meet five ordinary people who are each in the middle of their own search. Nadia bakes bread, Joseph drives a bus, Mei cleans hospital wards, Samuel has retired from a lifetime of engineering, and Grace is a schoolgirl who loves books. None of them is famous, and that is exactly the point, because their questions are probably very close to yours.

Each chapter of this book offers a single idea, a story to bring it to life and a small exercise to try before you turn the page. All you will need is a notebook, a pencil and a willingness to be honest with yourself. Read slowly, take as many days as you need over each chapter, and treat the exercises as invitations to be accepted rather than as homework to be marked.

For your first exercise, think back to the last time you felt truly useful, not impressive or admired but genuinely needed. Write down what you were doing, who was with you and what it was about the moment that made it feel so good. That small memory is a first thread, and the rest of this book will help you follow it.

Nadia wakes at four every morning, long before the street has stirred, and walks through the dark to her bakery. By the time the sun has climbed over the rooftops, the whole shop is filled with the smell of warm bread and the first customers are already waiting at the door. She has worked hard for all of this over many years, and the whole street loves her warmly for it.

Nadia owns a bakery that the whole street adores, and her accounts have never looked healthier. Even so, each evening she locks the door, switches off the ovens and stands for a moment in the dark with a strange, hollow feeling. She has everything she once wished for, and still something seems to be missing.

Ten years ago Nadia left a secure job in a vast factory kitchen and used her savings to open a small bakery of her own. She worked through the first lean winters, paid back every loan and gradually built the shop of her dreams. By any ordinary measure she has achieved nearly everything she set out to do.

Her friends tell her that she should be delighted with herself, and in her mind she agrees with every word they say. This only adds a layer of guilt on top of the emptiness, as though she were being ungrateful for a gift she cannot quite enjoy. She begins to wonder whether success and satisfaction are really the same thing after all.

Hoping to cure the problem, Nadia buys a gleaming new oven and books a short holiday by the sea. Each one gives her a flicker of pleasure that lasts for a few days, and then the old hollow feeling quietly returns. It seems that wants can be satisfied, but they cannot be made to feed something deeper.

One grey morning, Nadia notices an elderly man who always buys the cheapest day-old bread and counts his coins twice before he pays. On the following day she slips a fresh roll into his bag and says nothing about it. She walks home that evening feeling lighter and happier than she has felt for many months.

Over the following weeks Nadia learns that the old man is called Walter, and that he lives alone in a small flat on a modest pension. He spent most of his working life in a factory, and he is far too proud to ask for anything from anyone. She decides that the best help she can give him is the kind that does not look like help.

Every morning Nadia slips a fresh roll into Walter's paper bag without a word of explanation. He always notices, and he always tips his cap to her gravely, and yet neither of them ever mentions the extra gift. It is a small secret between two people, and it seems to make both of them stand a little taller.

One afternoon her young assistant Dev remarks, quite innocently, that Nadia always hums to herself whenever she gives something away. She stops with a loaf in her hands and realises, with a small shock, that he is right, and that these are the happiest moments of her working day. The money in the till has never once made her hum, whereas a loaf placed in the right pair of hands almost always does.

That night Nadia sits alone on a crate in the quiet back room and asks herself a question that she has never asked before. Who is this bakery really for, beyond herself and her accounts, and what might it become if she let the answer lead? She does not find the answer straight away, but simply asking the question feels like opening a window in a stuffy room.

Purpose rarely begins with a grand plan drawn up carefully at a desk by lamplight. More often it begins in the moment you look up from your own worries and truly see what someone near you is lacking. Attention, it turns out, is the doorway through which most meaningful work first enters a life.

Most of us move through the day with our eyes lowered to a glowing screen, and we miss a surprising amount of what is happening around us. To look up and truly see the person beside you is the first act of attention, and it costs nothing at all. Many people have walked past a need for years without ever noticing it was there.

For one whole week, Nadia walks along her street with her head held high and a small notebook in her coat pocket. She writes down everything that she notices, from the lonely and the hungry to the rushed and the weary. She has lived here for ten years, and she is astonished by how much she had never seen.

One afternoon a student counts her coins slowly and carefully, and in the end buys only the smallest loaf on the shelf. Later that week a young mother quietly gives her own lunch to her hungry child and takes nothing for herself, and Nadia begins to see a pattern. Many of her neighbours are managing on very little, and most of them would never say so aloud.

There are far too many needs in the world for any one person to meet, and trying to carry them all is a sure way to carry none. Look instead for the single need that touches your heart most deeply, the one that you cannot stop thinking about on the walk home. That persistent tug is no accident, and it is frequently the first stirring of a genuine vocation.

Here are three questions that are worth carrying around with you for a week. What troubles you deeply, what fills you with delight, and what do you possess that might be offered to the people who are affected? Where the three answers overlap, you will often find, faint but unmistakable, the outline of a purpose waiting to be drawn.

Instead of guessing what Walter might need, Nadia simply asks him what he likes best, and the question surprises him. He smiles for the first time in weeks and admits that he has always loved dark rye, which his wife used to bake on Sundays. Asking before helping turns a kindness from a mere favour into something much closer to a conversation between equals.

Nadia places a basket of fresh rolls beside the door with a short handwritten card propped against it. It invites anyone to take what they need and to leave what they can, and it asks no questions of anybody. In this way help can be given without making the person who receives it feel small.

A glance across a crowded room tells you very little about what another person truly needs. When you stop and listen to their story, the real need often rises to the surface, and it is rarely the one you expected. People are usually far more eager to be heard than they are to be helped, and the first is often the larger gift.

Your exercise for this chapter is to take a ten-minute walk through your own neighbourhood with your head up and your phone in your pocket. Write down three needs that you notice, then circle the one that tugs at you hardest and sit with it for a day. You are not obliged to solve anything yet, and the aim of the exercise is only to see clearly what has been in front of you all along.

Your gifts are the things that come so easily to you that you hardly notice them, while other people struggle for hours to do the same. They are valuable clues, since the abilities you were given usually point toward the kind of help you are best placed to offer. Ask your friends what they would come to you for, and listen carefully to the answer.

Our gifts can hide in plain sight, precisely because they come so easily that we assume everybody else must have them too. We tend to prize what cost us effort and to dismiss what flows from us naturally, which is almost the reverse of the truth. The thing you consider ordinary may be the very thing someone else has been praying for.

Nadia takes her own advice and asks Dev what he thinks people come to her for, expecting him to say bread. He thinks for a long moment and answers that she makes everyone who walks in feel as though they have come home. She had never once counted that as a skill, yet it is plainly the secret ingredient of her shop.

Gifts are not limited to the dazzling talents of music, sport or invention that attract applause. Patience, a sense of humour, a calm head in a crisis, a careful eye for detail and a good memory for names are every bit as precious. The world is held together largely by quiet gifts of this kind, which seldom win prizes.

Joseph has driven the number nine bus for eleven years, and he knows most of his regular passengers by name, their children's names and their favourite seats. His particular gift is a steady, unhurried kindness that makes a tired stranger feel welcome before the second stop. Nobody has ever called it a talent, and yet it quietly changes the mood of an entire morning.

Joseph begins his first journey at six each morning, when the number nine bus fills with nurses finishing nights, students clutching coffee and cleaners on their way to work. He knows where each of them will step off, what they study and how they take their tea. To them he is not simply a driver but the most reliable friendly face of the day.

One grey morning Joseph notices a passenger weeping quietly in a window seat, her face turned to the glass. He says nothing at all, but he lowers the radio, takes the corners a little more gently and lets the bus become a small moving room of privacy. Sometimes the most generous gift we can offer a stranger is simply to make a little space around her sorrow and leave it undisturbed.

A gift behaves very much like a muscle, growing stronger and more graceful with every use. If you tuck it away for fear of seeming proud or foolish, it slowly weakens and you may even forget that it was ever yours. The kindest thing you can do for your gift is to put it to work, imperfectly and often.

A loaf of bread is made to be broken and shared, and a gift of any kind is very much the same. Kept for yourself it becomes a private curiosity, but offered to others it turns into nourishment for a whole table. Ask not only what you are good at, but also who would be glad of it.

Your exercise is to write down three of your gifts, however modest or unfashionable they may seem to you. Beside each one, put the name of a particular person who could benefit from it this week, and then find a small way to offer it. A gift with a name beside it is far more likely to be given than a gift floating in the abstract.

Ordinary work can become a form of service once you keep in mind the people it touches, whatever your title or your pay. A spotless floor, a hot meal or a ticket handed over with a smile can ease another person's day more than any speech could. The work does not change, but your reason for doing it gives the same hours a very different weight.

Mei works the night shift at the hospital, pushing her trolley through long corridors that hum with the quiet sounds of machines. Hardly anyone notices a cleaner, and very few ever think to thank her, yet she is present at precisely the hour when fear runs highest. Her work is invisible, but its effects are felt by everyone who sleeps in those beds.

Mei spent a frightening year in hospital as a young woman, and some time later she took a job cleaning those very wards. She remembers exactly how long the nights felt and how lonely a waiting room can be, so she always pauses to speak to anxious families. Her own hard season did not become good, but it has become something she can offer.

One night Mei notices a family waiting outside the intensive ward, shivering in their thin coats and staring at the floor. She fetches a warm blanket from the store, sets it around the mother's shoulders and sits with them in silence for a minute. Nobody ever asked her to do this, and it is probably the most important thing she does all week.

There is one question that can transform almost any job, and it is simply this: who is this work for? Once you can picture the faces of the people who benefit, the work stops being merely a task to be completed and becomes a way of giving. The duties stay exactly the same, but they begin to carry a different weight.

Many jobs serve people who will never see your face or learn your name, whether it is farming, building, teaching or driving a lorry through the night. Each of them is a thread in the great web that keeps a town alive, and none of the threads is smaller than another. Honest work done carefully and with a clear conscience deserves real honour, whatever the pay may be or the title on the door.

Over the following days, Nadia begins to see her own work through entirely fresh and grateful eyes. She is not merely selling bread across a counter, she decides, but sending people out into a hard day with something warm in their hands and something kind in their hearts. The ovens, the flour and the alarm clock at four in the morning are exactly the same, but they now serve something.

A cheerful attitude cannot redeem a job whose purpose is to harm other people, and it would be a mistake to pretend otherwise. If your conscience keeps telling you that your work does damage, take that voice seriously, and look for an honest way to change course. Service has to point somewhere good in order to count as service at all.

If you cannot change your job at the moment, you can still change the manner in which you do it, and that is often where the real freedom lies. A warm greeting, a tidy desk left ready for the next person or a patient word to a difficult customer can all carry meaning. Small touches like these turn a duty into a gift without altering a single line of the job description.

For your exercise today, choose one ordinary task from your working day, whether it is answering an email, washing a pan or filing a report. Name the real person who will benefit from it, and then do it as though you were doing it for them alone. Notice, when you have finished, whether the very same hour feels any different from the hours that came before it.

Wants are restless and change with the season, so that what you craved passionately last spring may bore you by the autumn. Your values, such as honesty, courage or care for the vulnerable, are slower and deeper, which is exactly why a lasting purpose is best rooted in them.
